prompt: A `Choice` state has rules and no `Default`. An input arrives that no rule matches. What happens on AWS?
hint: `Default` is where everything else goes.

choices.text: The execution fails with `States.NoChoiceMatched`
choices.why: Yes. With no rule and no `Default`, there is nowhere to go.

choices.text: It follows the first rule's `Next`
choices.why: A rule is followed only when it matches.

choices.text: The execution succeeds, with its input as the output
choices.why: Only `Succeed` ends a run that way; a `Choice` is not an end state.

choices.text: It waits until an input that matches arrives
choices.why: A `Choice` reads the input it has once; it never waits.

prompt: Right after `start-execution`, `describe-execution` for `order-42` said `RUNNING`. Why?
hint: What does the caller wait for?

choices.text: moto is slower than AWS at starting executions
choices.why: AWS answers the same way: a Standard start returns before the work.

choices.text: The command line had not yet sent the input
choices.why: The input is part of the start call; it was already there.

choices.text: The start returns at once; the run goes on alone
choices.why: Yes. The two-second `Wait` and the task happened after the command returned.

choices.text: The queue was still empty, so `Notify` was retrying
choices.why: The queue existed; an empty queue is no error, and the history shows no retry.

prompt: `order-42` went through the `Wait` and its history had 13 events. `order-43` skipped it. A `Wait` adds one event on entering and one on leaving. How many events did `order-43` have?
hint: 13 minus what the Wait adds.

prompt: moto created a state machine whose only state has `"Next": "B"`, and no state `B` exists. What does AWS do with the same command?
hint: AWS checks a definition when it is created.

choices.text: Refuses it with `InvalidDefinition`
choices.why: Yes, naming the state that points nowhere.

choices.text: Creates it, and the first execution fails at `A`
choices.why: That is moto's behaviour at best; AWS never creates it.

choices.text: Creates it and treats `A` as an end state
choices.why: A missing `Next` target is an error, not an implicit end.

choices.text: Creates a `Pass` state called `B` to fill the gap
choices.why: Nothing is ever added to a definition for you.

prompt: Match each state type with what it does.
hint: One description belongs to a type not on the left.

pairs.right: reads the input and picks the next state
holds the execution and runs nothing
runs the same steps once per item of a list
runs different branches at once and waits for all

right_distractors: calls a service and takes its answer as the result

prompt: In the `Notify` state, `___` puts SQS's answer at `$.sent`, beside the input, instead of replacing the input with it.
hint: A field name, one word in two parts.

prompt: A Standard workflow of 8 steps runs 500,000 times a month, with no retries. At 37.5 USD per million state transitions, what does a month cost? Leave out the free tier.
hint: Executions × steps, then per million.

prompt: The same 500,000 runs as Express workflows take 1.5 s each at the smallest memory step, 64 MB. At 1 USD per million requests and 0.00001667 USD per GB-second, what does a month cost?
hint: 64 MB is 0.0625 GB; add the requests.

prompt: A refund workflow waits for a manager's approval, which takes up to two days. Which type does it need?
hint: Two limits rule one of them out.

choices.text: Express, because it is about a hundred times cheaper
choices.why: It cannot run past five minutes, and it has no `.waitForTaskToken`.

choices.text: Express, started synchronously from the API
choices.why: A synchronous start makes the caller wait; the five-minute limit still applies.

choices.text: Either; the type only changes the price
choices.why: The types differ in duration, history and the waits they support.

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Yes: a year of duration and the token callback.

prompt: In the lab, an Express state machine with a one-hour `Wait` succeeds after an hour. What would AWS do?
hint: What did `describe-state-machine` report for `orders-fast`?

choices.text: The same, since moto imitates AWS
choices.why: moto stored the machine as Standard, so it ran without Express's limit.

choices.text: Stop the execution at five minutes
choices.why: Yes. Express's limit is five minutes, and moto does not apply it.

choices.text: Refuse to create a machine containing a `Wait`
choices.why: Express accepts a `Wait`; the run as a whole is what is limited.

choices.text: Run it to the end and bill it as Standard
choices.why: The type is fixed at creation and decides both the limits and the bill.

prompt: Which of these are true of an Express workflow on AWS? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table in the section.

choices.text: Started asynchronously, it runs at least once
choices.why: Yes, so a run may repeat.

choices.text: Its history is readable from the service for 90 days
choices.why: That is Standard; Express sends history to CloudWatch Logs if logging is on.

choices.text: It has no `.waitForTaskToken`
choices.why: Yes; neither does it have `.sync`.

choices.text: It is billed per state transition
choices.why: Express is billed per request and by duration and memory.

choices.text: A run lasts five minutes at most
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: An Express workflow started asynchronously charges a card in one of its steps. A customer is charged twice for one order, and the workflow has no `Retry`. What explains it, and what prevents it?
hint: What does at least once allow?

choices.text: A hidden default `Retry`; add `MaxAttempts: 0`
choices.why: There is no default retry on a task; the repeat came from the execution.

choices.text: The customer clicked twice; Express cannot be the cause
choices.why: It can: at-least-once execution is part of what Express promises.

choices.text: Express runs every step twice; switch to a synchronous start
choices.why: It does not run every step twice; it may run the whole workflow again. Synchronous is at most once, which can lose a run instead.

choices.text: It ran twice; pass the provider an idempotency key
choices.why: Yes. Async Express is at least once, so the charge must recognise a repeat.

prompt: A `Retry` has `IntervalSeconds: 3`, `BackoffRate: 2` and `MaxAttempts: 3`, and every attempt fails at once. How many seconds pass waiting between attempts, in total, before the `Catch` takes over?
hint: Three retries; each gap is twice the last.

prompt: Put the events of `order-45` in the order they happened.
hint: `MaxAttempts: 2` means two retries after the first try.
trap: The `Catch` acts only after the last retry, not after the first failure.

prompt: `order-45` failed while sending to SQS, yet `describe-execution` reported the error `NotifyFailed`. Why?
hint: Where did the `Catch` send the execution?

choices.text: moto renames SQS errors
choices.why: moto kept SQS's error on the task events; the name came from the document.

choices.text: The execution ended in a `Fail` state, which names its own error
choices.why: Yes. The SQS error is still in the `TaskFailed` events.

choices.text: `States.ALL` turns every error into `NotifyFailed`
choices.why: `States.ALL` only matches errors; it renames nothing.

choices.text: Only the last attempt's error is ever kept
choices.why: Each failed attempt is in the history with its own error.

prompt: A task's `Retry` list has `States.ALL` first, then `States.Timeout` with a longer interval. What is wrong?
hint: Rules are tried in order.

choices.text: Nothing; the more specific rule wins wherever it is
choices.why: Rules are tried in order and the first match wins.

choices.text: A timeout cannot be retried
choices.why: `States.Timeout` can be retried like any error.

choices.text: `States.ALL` has to come last, so AWS refuses the definition
choices.why: Yes. It is the catch-all, and anything after it could never be reached.

choices.text: `States.Timeout` is only valid inside a `Catch`
choices.why: Error names work in both `Retry` and `Catch`.

prompt: A payment step has a `Retry`. Which value should it send to the payment provider as the idempotency key?
hint: It has to be the same on every attempt of the same work.

choices.text: `$$.Execution.Name`
choices.why: Yes. Unique per execution and unchanged between retries.

choices.text: A new UUID generated on each attempt
choices.why: Then each retry looks like a new payment, which is the problem.

choices.text: The time the attempt started
choices.why: It changes on every attempt.

choices.text: `$$.Task.Token`
choices.why: A token exists only for callback tasks, and it is a handle, not a key.

prompt: Set to `FULL`, the retry field `___` randomises each gap, so that a thousand executions failing together do not all try again in the same second.
hint: Two words joined, in the style of `BackoffRate`.

prompt: On a Standard workflow, how does a `Wait` of a week compare in price with a `Wait` of one second?
hint: What does Standard bill?

choices.text: A week costs about 600,000 times more
choices.why: Standard bills transitions, not time spent in a state.

choices.text: The same
choices.why: Yes. The state is the same transitions, and the time is free.

choices.text: A week is refused; a `Wait` lasts five minutes at most
choices.why: Five minutes is Express's limit for a whole run, not a `Wait`'s on Standard.

choices.text: A week costs one transition per hour waited
choices.why: A wait does not tick; it is entered once and left once.

prompt: A `.waitForTaskToken` task has `TimeoutSeconds: 86400` and `HeartbeatSeconds: 300`. The worker sends one heartbeat, then crashes. When does the task fail, and with what?
hint: Which of the two limits runs out first?

choices.text: After about five minutes, with `States.HeartbeatTimeout`
choices.why: Yes. Silence longer than `HeartbeatSeconds` fails the task.

choices.text: After a day, with `States.Timeout`
choices.why: The heartbeat limit runs out long before the day does.

choices.text: Never: a worker that crashed leaves it waiting for a whole year
choices.why: Both limits are set, and either ends the wait.

choices.text: At once, with `States.TaskFailed`
choices.why: Nobody tells Step Functions about a crash; it notices the silence.

prompt: Match each piece of work with the way the state should wait for it.
hint: Who decides that the wait is over?

pairs.left: send a reminder at the hour the customer chose
an ECS task that must finish before the next step
start a report nobody waits for

right_distractors: an Express workflow with a long `Wait`

prompt: The store's system receives a message carrying a task token from AWS. What should it do with the token?
hint: It is up to 1,024 characters and meant to be opaque.

choices.text: Read the order id out of it
choices.why: Nothing in it is meant to be read; the order travels beside it in the message.

choices.text: Shorten it to a UUID, as moto's tokens are
choices.why: moto's tokens are short; AWS's are not, and a cut token matches nothing.

choices.text: Pass it to `start-execution` to resume the workflow
choices.why: That starts a new execution; the waiting one resumes only on a send-task call.

choices.text: Store it whole and send it back
choices.why: Yes, with `send-task-success` or `send-task-failure`. It is a handle on one waiting task, and nothing more.

prompt: Every photo uploaded to S3 becomes three thumbnails: 200,000 photos a day, each done in under three seconds, and a repeat only overwrites the same three files. Which type of workflow fits?
hint: Short, many, and safe to repeat.

choices.text: Standard, because it runs exactly once
choices.why: Exactly once buys nothing when a repeat is harmless, and it costs per transition.

choices.text: Express
choices.why: Yes: under five minutes, many runs, and idempotent by nature.

choices.text: Standard with `.waitForTaskToken` on each thumbnail
choices.why: Nobody hands a token back here; the work is the service's own.

choices.text: Neither: a state machine cannot be started by S3
choices.why: An EventBridge rule on the upload starts one, as lesson 21 shows.

prompt: Which of these did the lab of this lesson really show? Choose all that apply.
hint: moto ran the interpreter; some AWS behaviour it skips.

choices.text: Retry gaps of one and then two real seconds
choices.why: Yes, in the timestamps of `order-45`.

choices.text: An Express execution stopped at five minutes
choices.why: moto stored the machine as Standard and applies no such limit.

choices.text: A task token handed back, and the execution finishing
choices.why: Yes, `order-46`.

choices.text: A broken definition refused with `InvalidDefinition`
choices.why: moto created `broken`; the refusal is AWS's documented behaviour.

choices.text: A message sent to SQS by a `Task`, with no function

prompt: A Standard workflow of 6 steps runs 100,000 times a month, and on average one step is retried twice per execution. At 37.5 USD per million transitions, what does the month cost?
